lines: Memory-map a real file, and also keep a separate, hand-built cache of those same bytes in your own code.
Does the mapped data end up resident in memory once, or does it genuinely end up resident twice?
answer: Twice — both copies are resident at the same time.
The kernel's own page cache and your application's own cache know absolutely nothing of each other.

lines: Run it for real: the mapped file's own pages stayed resident in the kernel's own page cache.
And reading that exact same file again, into a separate application cache, genuinely grew memory by roughly another full copy.
Open that same file bypassing the page cache entirely, and read it into a buffer that isn't aligned to a block boundary.
Does that read quietly degrade, silently succeed, or fail outright with a specific error?
answer: It fails outright, with a specific, clear error.
Bypassing the cache never silently fixes a misaligned buffer for you.

lines: Run it for real: the misaligned read failed outright with that exact clear error.
And the very same read, with a properly aligned buffer instead, succeeded cleanly.
steps.takeaway: Direct I/O removes the double copy only by making every buffer's alignment the caller's own strict job.

lines: If a mapped page's real read genuinely fails — a bad sector, a disk gone missing entirely —
does the program get back a normal, recoverable error?
answer: No — it can raise a process-terminating signal outright.
A page fault simply has no normal error channel to hand a result back through.

lines: The paper's own argument names exactly four real costs: a dirty page written back whenever the kernel chooses, not the database.
A stall with no promised end. A crash instead of a result to handle. And every other thread paused just to unmap one region.
steps.takeaway: Mapping a file trades an explicit result for four real failure modes most systems can't actually afford.

lines: Given every one of those four real costs, is there still ever a real system where mapping a file directly is the right call?
Or is it simply never worth it?
answer: Yes — a read-mostly workload with no bounded-latency need at all.
That is exactly the one case a well-known embedded database is built around.

lines: The paper's own recommendation is exactly that narrow: mapping stays the right call when the working set fits in memory and the workload is read-only.
Which is precisely the case that well-known embedded database's own design is built around.
So, pulling this together: holding bytes twice, a strict alignment cost, and four named failure classes are really the same question, asked three times.
Who decides when a page actually moves, and does the caller ever find out if that goes wrong.
steps.takeaway: An owned buffer pool exists because most systems need an explicit answer that mapping leaves to the kernel.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: a mapped file genuinely holds the same bytes twice, the moment an application keeps its own cache on top.
Direct access genuinely removes that only by making every buffer's alignment the caller's own strict job.
And the paper's own four failure classes are exactly why most databases own their buffer pool instead — except for that one narrow, read-mostly exception.
